skills.name: Describe stationary waves, harmonics and overtones

note.text:
A stationary (standing) wave is made when two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions and interfere, usually a wave and its own reflection.
Nodes are points that never move (destructive interference). Antinodes are points that vibrate most (constructive interference).
The distance between two neighbouring nodes is half a wavelength: λ = 2 × (node-to-node distance).
On a string of length L fixed at both ends there must be a node at each end, so L = nλ/2, that is λ = 2L/n with n = 1, 2, 3, …
n = 1 is the fundamental or first harmonic, with frequency f₁. n = 2 is the second harmonic (first overtone), with frequency 2f₁, and so on.
Unlike a progressive wave, a stationary wave carries no energy along the string.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to explain how a stationary wave is formed, find λ from the node spacing or the number of loops, and name the harmonics.
Builds on: Lesson {11} (interference and reflection) and Lesson {10} (v = fλ).
Leads to: Lesson {15} (vibrating strings) and the notes made by musical instruments.

sections.heading: Nodes, antinodes and loops
sections.text:
Send a wave along a string fixed at the far end. The reflected wave meets the wave still going forward. Where they are always out of step, the string never moves: a node. Where they are always in step, it vibrates most: an antinode.
The pattern stays in one place, so it is a stationary wave. Unlike a progressive wave, it carries no energy along the string.
Each loop between two nodes is half a wavelength long, so:
λ = {2} × (distance from one node to the next).
A string fixed at both ends must have a node at each end, so a whole number of loops must fit: L = nλ ÷ {2}, that is λ = {2}L ÷ n.

sections.heading: Harmonics and overtones
sections.text:
With n = {1}, the string vibrates as one loop. This is the fundamental, or first harmonic: λ₁ = {2}L and f₁ = v ÷ ({2}L).
• n = {2}: two loops, λ = L, frequency {2}f₁. Second harmonic, also called the first overtone.
• n = {3}: three loops, λ = {2}L ÷ {3}, frequency {3}f₁. Third harmonic, second overtone.
So the nth harmonic has n loops, n + {1} nodes, n antinodes and frequency n × f₁.
A plucked guitar string vibrates in several of these at once; the mixture gives the instrument its quality.

key_words.meaning: a wave pattern that stays in place, made by two waves meeting
the lowest frequency, with one loop
a frequency that is a whole number times the fundamental

mistake.wrong: the distance between neighbouring nodes is one wavelength
mistake.why: A full wave has two loops: one above the line and one below.

worked_example.problem: A string of length {L} m fixed at both ends vibrates in {n} loops. Find the wavelength.
steps: Each loop is half a wavelength long.

cards.idea: A node never moves; an antinode vibrates most. Neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart.
example: nodes {0.2} m apart means λ = {0.4} m

cards.idea: On a string fixed at both ends, λ = {2}L/n, where n is the number of loops.
example: L = {0.6} m with {3} loops: λ = {0.4} m

cards.idea: The nth harmonic has frequency n × the fundamental.
example: f₁ = {100} Hz gives a third harmonic of {300} Hz

check.prompt: A string has a fundamental frequency of {f1} Hz. Find the frequency of its {n}{n == 2 ? 'nd' : n == 3 ? 'rd' : 'th'} harmonic, in hertz.

misconceptions.explain: A higher harmonic has a HIGHER frequency: multiply.
The {n}th harmonic is {n} × f₁. ({n} × f₁ is also called the {n - 1}{n - 1 == 1 ? 'st' : n - 1 == 2 ? 'nd' : n - 1 == 3 ? 'rd' : 'th'} overtone.)

solution: The nth harmonic has n times the fundamental frequency.

questions.prompt: On a stationary wave, two neighbouring nodes are {d} cm apart. Find the wavelength, in cm.

misconceptions.explain: {d} cm is only half a wavelength.
Multiply by {2}: node to node is HALF a wavelength.

solution: The distance between neighbouring nodes is half a wavelength.

questions.prompt: A string of length {L} m fixed at both ends vibrates in {n} loops. Find the wavelength, in metres.

misconceptions.explain: Each loop is HALF a wavelength, so λ = {2}L ÷ n.
That is the wavelength of the fundamental, with one loop. Here there are {n}.

solution: Each loop is half a wavelength, and {n} loops fill the string.

questions.prompt: A string has a fundamental frequency of {f1} Hz. Find the frequency of its {n}{n == 2 ? 'nd' : n == 3 ? 'rd' : 'th'} harmonic, in hertz.

misconceptions.explain: A higher harmonic has a HIGHER frequency: multiply.
The {n}th harmonic is {n} × f₁. ({n} × f₁ is also called the {n - 1}{n - 1 == 1 ? 'st' : n - 1 == 2 ? 'nd' : n - 1 == 3 ? 'rd' : 'th'} overtone.)

solution: The nth harmonic has n times the fundamental frequency.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a string fixed at both ends vibrating as a stationary wave. How many nodes and antinodes are there?

misconceptions.explain: The ends are fixed, so they are nodes: there is always one node more than the number of loops.
Count the ends: a string fixed at both ends has a node at each end.
Neighbouring loops share a node, so they are not counted twice.

solution: Each loop has one antinode in the middle, so there are {n} antinodes.
There is a node at each end and one between each pair of loops: {n} + {1} = {n + 1}.

pick.q: How does a stationary wave differ from a progressive wave?
pick.r: A stationary wave has fixed nodes and carries no energy along; a progressive wave carries energy forward
w: A stationary wave has a higher frequency
A stationary wave has no amplitude
There is no difference; the names mean the same thing
e: The two waves that make a stationary wave have the same frequency as it does.
The antinodes have a large amplitude; only the nodes do not move.
They behave quite differently: one carries energy away, the other does not.
pick.y: In a stationary wave the pattern stays where it is, with the energy stored in the vibration.

pick.q: What is needed to make a stationary wave?
pick.r: Two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travelling in opposite directions
w: Two waves of different frequencies travelling the same way
One wave of very large amplitude
Two waves travelling the same way at different speeds
e: Different frequencies give a pattern that will not stay still.
A single wave travelling along is a progressive wave, however large.
Waves going the same way cannot make fixed nodes.
pick.y: Usually a wave and its own reflection meet and interfere, giving fixed nodes and antinodes.

pick.q: In a stationary wave, how does the amplitude vary along the string?
pick.r: It is zero at the nodes and greatest at the antinodes
w: It is the same everywhere, as in a progressive wave
It is greatest at the nodes
It falls steadily from one end to the other
e: Equal amplitude everywhere is what happens in a progressive wave.
A node is a point that never moves, so its amplitude is zero.
The amplitude rises and falls repeatedly along the string.
pick.y: Nodes are points of destructive interference and antinodes points of constructive interference.

pick.q: Why does a stationary wave on a string carry no energy along the string?
pick.r: The nodes never move, so no energy can pass through them
w: The string is too short to carry energy
The energy is destroyed at the nodes
The wave has no amplitude anywhere
e: Length is not the reason; a long string behaves the same way.
Energy is never destroyed; here it stays stored in the vibrating loops.
The antinodes vibrate with a large amplitude.
pick.y: Energy is stored in each loop, moving between kinetic and potential, but it does not travel past a node.
